# Mission Canvas

> Customized Software as a Service. Mission Canvas builds software around your business workflows, then maintains and improves it as your work changes.

Mission Canvas offers Customized Software as a Service: software built around a business workflow, with scoped maintenance and agreed improvements. A reusable foundation supports source-linked work, version history and controlled actions. Each engagement defines its workflow, costs, deployment and care responsibilities. Start a workflow conversation: https://pretendhome.github.io/audit/

The work between the apps

## That process everyone works around? Start there.
The spreadsheet beside the CRM. The email someone copies into a form. The person who always knows what happens next.
That is where we start. We understand the job, build software around it and take responsibility for its ongoing care.
Purpose-built for your business, on a common foundation we can maintain and extend.
What could we build for you?

## One workflow.
A better way through.
Start small enough to see the difference. These examples show the kinds of work we can scope together.
01 Client onboarding From a new enquiry to a clear, ready-to-review brief. 02 Quotes & proposals Turn approved information into a proposal your team can use. 03 Scheduling & follow-up Keep the next step from getting lost between the inbox and calendar.
Client onboarding ILLUSTRATIVE
- 1
Receive the request
Bring selected forms, emails and files into one workflow.
- 2
Prepare the work
Assemble a brief and show what information is still missing.
- 3
Review and respond
Let the responsible person check the draft and request the next action.
↳ A prepared response, with its sources and history.
The full workflow, connected tools and permissions are agreed for each implementation.
Quotes & proposals ILLUSTRATIVE
- 1
Gather the inputs
Use the rate sheets, notes and project documents you choose.
- 2
Build the proposal
Apply the agreed structure and keep internal information separate.
- 3
Check and send
Review the version, make changes and record the final communication.
↳ A proposal built around your rules and reviewed by your team.
The full workflow, connected tools and permissions are agreed for each implementation.
Scheduling & follow-up ILLUSTRATIVE
- 1
Understand the request
Bring the incoming message together with permitted calendar information.
- 2
Prepare the next step
Draft a response or a scheduling change for the right person.
- 3
Keep the record
Record what was requested and surface an uncertain result for review.
↳ A clear next step, with a record of what happened.
The full workflow, connected tools and permissions are agreed for each implementation.

A few good questions

## Before we start.
More answers
What does CSaaS mean?
Customized Software as a Service. We build software around a specific business workflow, then provide ongoing maintenance and agreed improvements. The service continues after the first release. How is this different from a custom development project?
The ongoing relationship is part of the offer. We agree what to build, how to check it and what care it needs. Maintenance and improvements have a defined scope rather than an open-ended promise. Do we have to replace our existing tools?
We start with the workflow and the systems you use. Some projects connect existing tools; others replace a small, awkward step. We scope the right boundary together. What will it cost?
We quote the initial work and the recurring care separately, against an agreed scope. Hosting, outside services and substantial new work are identified in the proposal. There is no published flat price yet.
Start with the real work

Built around the people doing the work

# Useful software needs someone responsible for its life.
Mission Canvas brings custom software development and ongoing care together around the workflows a business needs to carry out every day.
01

## Start by understanding the business.
The starting point is the work itself: who needs an answer, which information matters, and what happens when something goes wrong.
We use those details to define a focused software project with a recognizable outcome and a practical way to review it.
02

## Build on a foundation that can be reused.
Common needs such as access, source references, document history, and connected services can share infrastructure while the workflow receives custom attention.
That approach gives the team a consistent starting point and leaves room for the details that make your business work differently.
03

## Make responsibility visible.
An engagement names the people responsible for business decisions, delivery, acceptance, and ongoing care, with a clear route for raising problems.
Your agreement should make it easy to understand what is included, who can approve changes, and how responsibilities end or transfer.
Your next step

## Tell us about the work.
Bring one workflow your team wants to improve, along with the people, tools, and decisions that make it matter.
Let’s talk about your work

A starting point for the conversation

# Different businesses need different details.
Explore illustrative workflows by industry, then use them to describe the information, people, and decisions your own software needs to support.
01

## Start from a familiar situation.
A construction handover, school administration request, delivery exception, and venue booking each involve different responsibilities, information, and points for human judgment.
The examples here help frame a useful conversation; a project's capabilities and delivery scope must be agreed for the actual business.

### Operational coordination
Construction, logistics, and office workflows can begin with repeated handoffs, incomplete records, and the work needed to keep people informed.

### People and requests
Education, front desk, and venue workflows can begin with incoming questions, required information, and decisions that need a responsible owner.

### Sensitive administration
Healthcare administration requires careful scoping of information, access, professional responsibilities, and applicable review before deciding whether a workflow is suitable.
02

## Reuse the foundation, define the business rules.
Common capabilities can share infrastructure, while your people, documents, permissions, decisions, and operating exceptions shape the custom software built around it.
Each engagement should name the first useful outcome and the evidence your team needs before putting that workflow into everyday use.
03

## Plan for changing requirements.
An ongoing care agreement gives maintenance, support, and agreed improvements a defined place as your business processes and connected systems change.
These industry pages describe possible scopes for discussion, not finished applications, existing client deployments, or guarantees about a particular business result.
Explore a starting point
Construction workflows Education workflows Logistics workflows Front desk workflows Events and venue workflows Healthcare administration workflows Office workflows
Your next step

## Bring the details that make your work different.
Choose a familiar example and tell us which people, systems, rules, and exceptions the workflow needs to handle for your business.

Source: https://pretendhome.github.io/canvases/construction

Illustrative workflow · Construction

# Keep project handoffs connected to the right information.
A custom construction workflow could connect selected project records, open questions, and handover tasks, with ongoing care defined for the solution. Illustrative setting. Workflow details and implementation are scoped with each business.
01

## A possible scope: preparing a project handover.
A workspace could bring approved project documents, outstanding items, and responsible owners together so the team can prepare a consistent handover package.
The scope would define document sources, required information, revision rules, and who can decide that an item is ready to close.

### Project records
Identify the drawings, forms, correspondence, and other approved sources needed for the handover, with clear treatment of missing or superseded material.

### Open items
Give outstanding questions an owner and status, with the supporting information needed for the responsible person to decide the next step.

### Review and issue
Define who reviews the package, which version is issued, and what record the team needs of the final communication or handoff.
02

## Build around the team's real responsibilities.
Different projects have different approval structures and document systems, so permissions and integrations need assessment before the workflow can be committed.
The software would support the agreed administrative process, with technical judgments and contractual decisions remaining with the people responsible for them.
03

## Keep the workflow useful as projects change.
Ongoing care could cover maintenance, support, and agreed adjustments to forms, document requirements, and connected systems as the operating process evolves.
This is an illustrative scope for discussion, not a completed construction product or evidence of an existing customer deployment or outcome.
Your next step

## Walk us through one project handoff.
Show where the documents come from, who needs to review them, and what your team must know before the handoff is complete.
Let’s talk about your work

Source: https://pretendhome.github.io/canvases/education

Illustrative workflow · Education

# Give recurring administration a clearer path.
A custom education workflow could bring requests, required information, and reviewed communications together, with access and ongoing care shaped around your setting.
01

## A possible scope: coordinating an administrative request.
A workspace could help staff collect the information needed for a recurring request, identify missing documents, and prepare a response for review.
The scope would define which records are appropriate, who may see them, and which decisions need an authorized member of staff.

### Request intake
Agree the information needed at the start, with practical guidance for incomplete submissions and a named person responsible for follow-up.

### Staff preparation
Bring permitted information together to help staff prepare the next step, with source references and clear handling of conflicting records.

### Reviewed communication
Define who checks a message, who is authorized to send it, and what the school or organization needs to retain afterward.
02

## Respect the setting and its responsibilities.
Student information, family communications, and safeguarding concerns require explicit access rules and specialist review of the proposed handling before use begins.
The software would support the agreed administrative task, while professional, safeguarding, and educational decisions remain with the people responsible for them.
03

## Adapt the workflow through an agreed care process.
Ongoing care could address maintenance, support, and agreed changes to forms, responsibilities, or connected systems as the organization's administrative needs evolve.
This example describes a possible engagement scope and does not represent a finished education application or an existing customer case study.
Your next step

## Start with one recurring administrative task.
Tell us who handles it, what information they need, and which decisions or communications must stay with an authorized person.

Illustrative workflow · Events and venues

# Bring an inquiry closer to a complete booking brief.
A custom venue workflow could connect incoming inquiries, event requirements, selected availability information, and reviewed proposals, with ongoing care agreed for the solution.
01

## A possible scope: preparing an event proposal.
A workspace could gather the client's requirements, show missing details, and prepare a proposal from the venue's approved packages and operating information.
The scope would define availability sources, pricing rules, review responsibilities, and the conditions that make an inquiry ready for a formal booking decision.

### A useful inquiry brief
Collect the event details the team needs to assess a request, with a clear owner for missing information and follow-up questions.

### Approved proposal material
Use the agreed packages, terms, and information sources to prepare a draft that the responsible person can check and revise before sending.

### An operational handoff
Define the information needed by the people delivering the event, including the status and owner of any requirements still awaiting a decision.
02

## Keep commitments with the right person.
Availability, pricing, contractual terms, and customer promises need explicit rules and authority, especially when the workflow connects to a booking or payment system.
Any proposed integration requires assessment of the existing tools, account permissions, and uncertainty around records that may change outside the custom application.
03

## Support the workflow through changing seasons.
Ongoing care could include maintenance, support, and agreed changes to packages, documents, responsibilities, or connected systems as the venue's operating needs evolve.
This example is a possible scope for a custom engagement, not an existing venue product, customer story, or promise of increased bookings.
Your next step

## Start with one inquiry and its handoffs.
Show how it becomes a proposal and booking brief, including the information, people, and decisions needed along the way.

Illustrative workflow · Healthcare administration

# Scope administrative support with clear professional boundaries.
A possible healthcare administration engagement would begin with the information, access, professional responsibilities, and review required before considering a custom software solution. Illustrative setting. Workflow details and implementation are scoped with each business.
01

## A possible scope: organizing an administrative request.
A workspace could help authorized staff gather an agreed set of administrative documents, identify missing information, and prepare a request for the responsible reviewer.
The first scope would define the task carefully, including the information it requires and the clinical or professional decisions that remain outside it.

### A bounded task
Identify the administrative outcome, the authorized staff involved, and the circumstances in which the workflow must pause for professional review or clarification.

### Defined information handling
Assess the data, access, retention, processing locations, and service providers involved before determining whether the proposed implementation is appropriate for the setting.

### A responsible reviewer
Agree who checks the work, which records are needed, and how staff escalate missing information or a result that cannot be trusted.
02

## Assess suitability before making an operating commitment.
Applicable privacy, security, contractual, and regulatory requirements need qualified review and explicit acceptance for the proposed implementation before sensitive information is used.
This site makes no healthcare compliance, certification, diagnostic, or clinical decision claim; the illustrative task concerns administrative coordination under appropriate human responsibility.
03

## Define the ongoing responsibilities precisely.
Any care agreement would need to explain maintenance, support, access changes, outside dependencies, and the handling of incidents within the accepted scope.
This is a possible workflow to assess for suitability, not a finished healthcare product, existing patient deployment, or evidence of clinical outcomes.
Your next step

## Begin with the administrative task and its boundaries.
Describe the workflow and required controls using non-sensitive examples, so the first discussion can focus on suitability and responsible scoping.
Let’s talk about your work

Illustrative workflow · Logistics

# Make delivery exceptions easier to coordinate.
A custom logistics workflow could connect selected shipment information, exception ownership, and customer updates, with ongoing care agreed around the operation.
01

## A possible scope: handling a delivery exception.
A workspace could gather the available shipment record, show the information still missing, and give the exception a responsible owner for follow-up.
The scope would define which systems supply status, how current that information must be, and what happens when sources disagree or stop updating.

### A shared view
Bring the agreed shipment information and supporting messages into one view, with clear source references and visible gaps in the record.

### An owned next step
Assign responsibility for investigating the exception and define which decisions the software can support within the agreed operating process and permissions.

### A reviewed update
Prepare a customer or partner update using approved information, with the review and sending authority your business requires for that communication.
02

## Make the integration limits visible.
Carrier interfaces, tracking availability, account permissions, and update delays need assessment before committing to the behavior of any proposed connection or notification.
Operational decisions and customer commitments stay with the responsible team, with uncertainty shown clearly when the software cannot establish a reliable status.
03

## Care for the connections the operation depends on.
Ongoing care could include maintenance, support, and agreed adjustments when external systems, message formats, or the team's exception handling process change.
This is an illustrative workflow for scoping, not an existing logistics product, live tracking guarantee, or claim of measured delivery improvement.
Your next step

## Describe one exception your team handles repeatedly.
Bring the messages, systems, and decisions involved so we can discuss a useful first scope and the care it would need.

Illustrative workflow · Office operations

# Give recurring office work a clear home.
A custom office workflow could connect requests, selected documents, responsible owners, and reviewed responses, with ongoing care defined around the team's needs. Illustrative setting. Workflow details and implementation are scoped with each business.
01

## A possible scope: coordinating an internal request.
A workspace could gather a request and its supporting documents, show what is missing, and help the responsible person prepare the next step.
The scope would define the information sources, business rules, review requirements, and records needed to understand how the request was handled and completed.

### A complete starting point
Agree the details needed for a useful request and make it clear who follows up when important information is missing.

### An owned decision
Bring the relevant information to the person responsible for the decision, with a clear boundary around what the software may prepare or change.

### A recorded outcome
Define the response, update, or handoff that completes the task, along with the activity record your team needs to find afterward.
02

## Work with the tools your team already depends on.
Email, calendars, document stores, and other business systems can be assessed for integration, with access and external account responsibilities agreed during scoping.
The first version should have a focused purpose, so the team can review it against representative work before adding more tasks or systems.
03

## Keep the software aligned with the office.
Ongoing care could cover maintenance, support, and agreed improvements as staff responsibilities, forms, business rules, and connected services change over time.
This is an illustrative custom engagement scope, not an existing office application, customer case study, or promise of a particular productivity gain.

Illustrative workflow · Front desk

# Connect an incoming question with a responsible next step.
A custom front desk workflow could help staff capture requests, find approved information, and coordinate follow-up, with voice considered where it proves useful.
01

## A possible scope: preparing a request for follow-up.
A workspace could help the front desk collect the details needed for a request and prepare a clear handoff to the responsible team.
The scope would define the questions, approved answers, routing rules, and situations that need a person to take over or make a decision.

### Capture the essentials
Agree which details are needed to understand the request, what consent is required, and how staff correct an incomplete or mistaken record.

### Use approved information
Identify the answers and source material that staff may rely on, with a clear route when the information does not cover the question.

### Make the handoff clear
Give the request an owner, show the agreed next step, and define how the team records that follow-up has actually happened.
02

## Treat voice as an implementation choice.
Any proposed voice interface needs testing with the actual equipment, environment, language needs, and interruptions that the front desk will encounter during use.
A voice feature should have clear limits and a practical handoff to people; this example makes no promise of unattended call handling.
03

## Keep information and routing current.
Ongoing care could cover maintenance, support, and agreed updates as opening hours, staff responsibilities, service information, or connected systems change over time.
This page presents an illustrative scope for discussion, not a completed reception product, proven voice service, or existing customer deployment claim.

Understand your software and its care

# Documentation should help your team get work done.
A service engagement needs clear workflow guidance, operating responsibilities, and a record of agreed changes, alongside any underlying application documentation.
01

## For a Mission Canvas service engagement.
Your project documentation should describe the agreed workflow, supported tasks, connected systems, permissions, and the situations that need a person's attention.
It should also explain how your team reports a problem, requests a change, and finds the current delivery and care scope.

### Using the workflow
Practical guidance should follow the tasks people need to carry out, including the exceptions and limitations they may encounter.

### Running the software
Operating guidance should identify account responsibilities, relevant dependencies, agreed maintenance arrangements, and the route for support when something needs attention.

### Reviewing changes
A change record should explain what changed, why it changed, and what your team needs to review or do next.
02

## For the Palette desktop application.
Palette has its own application guidance, installation requirements, and operating limits that should be checked for the environment you plan to use.
Those materials describe the desktop foundation; the managed service agreement separately defines your business workflow, delivery responsibilities, and ongoing care.
03

## Keep the current agreement easy to find.
Public guidance introduces the approach, while project documents should record the precise behavior, access arrangements, and responsibilities agreed for your solution.
When a change affects those arrangements, the documentation and acceptance criteria should be updated alongside the software your team will use.

Understanding the service

# A clearer picture of custom software with ongoing care.
These answers describe our proposed CSaaS approach; your written proposal sets the scope, responsibilities, price, and operating terms for an engagement.
01

## What does CSaaS mean here?
Customized Software as a Service brings software built around your workflow together with an agreement for its maintenance, support, and improvement.
The solution combines reusable infrastructure with custom development, while the engagement defines the ongoing responsibilities your particular workflow needs clearly.
02

## What kinds of work are a useful starting point?
Start with recurring work that crosses documents, messages, spreadsheets, or systems, especially when people spend time coordinating the same information repeatedly.
A focused first scope makes the software easier to review and helps establish the evidence needed for any later expansion.
03

## What gets agreed before work begins?
The proposal should cover the workflow, delivery scope, acceptance criteria, commercial terms, data handling, support arrangements, and ownership or access rights.
It should also explain third-party costs, changes outside scope, and how the software and relevant information can be handed over.
A little more detail

## Questions worth asking.
Does every project use AI?
AI is an implementation choice where it helps the workflow; ordinary software, clear rules, and human review may be more appropriate. Can you work with our existing systems?
We assess the systems, available interfaces, account permissions, and vendor constraints during scoping before committing to a particular integration or behavior. Can the software take actions by itself?
Any delegated action needs an agreed scope, authority, and review policy; we make no general promise of unattended or autonomous operation. How long will a project take?
Delivery timing depends on scope, integrations, access, review availability, and unresolved requirements, and belongs in the proposal for your project. Who owns the software and information?
Ownership, licensing, data access, export, and handover rights must be explained in the written agreement before you commit to an engagement. What if our workflow changes?
We review the request together and determine whether it fits recurring care or needs a separately agreed build scope and quote.
Your next step

## Start with the situation you have.
You can bring an awkward spreadsheet, a repeated handoff, or a recurring task and describe what should happen instead.
Let’s talk about your work

From workflow to working software

# Start with the work your team needs to do.
We shape a focused software project around your workflow, then agree how its maintenance and improvement will be handled.
Understand

## Follow one real piece of work.
We start with a recurring task, the people involved, the information they need, and the outcome they consider complete.
Together, we identify the awkward handoffs, repeated entry, missing information, and decisions that still need a responsible person's judgment.

### A clear outcome
Describe what should happen when the workflow succeeds, including the records and communications your team needs at the end.

### An agreed boundary
Choose the people, systems, information, and actions included in the first scope, with exceptions that everyone can understand.

### A named owner
Identify who can answer business questions, judge the result, and authorize any changes that affect customers or other teams.
Build

## Make the result concrete enough to judge.
We build around the agreed workflow, using a reusable foundation for common needs and custom development for your particular requirements.
Your team reviews the software against representative work, including exceptions, before we agree what belongs in everyday use together.
Care

## Plan for the life after launch.
The care agreement defines responsibility for maintenance, support, dependencies, and improvements, with a clear route for reporting problems and requesting changes.
As your workflow changes, we review priorities together and agree which adjustments fit the existing scope or need a separate quote.
Your next step

## Bring one recurring workflow.
Show us where the work starts, where it gets stuck, and what your team needs to happen next.
Let’s talk about your work

The desktop foundation

# A desktop application behind the workflow work.
Palette is a desktop foundation and development application associated with Mission Canvas, with its own capabilities, installation requirements, and operating boundaries.
01

## A foundation for building and reviewing work.
Its development brings together mechanisms for source-linked documents, versioned changes, scoped access, connected services, and records of actions and outcomes.
A mechanism's presence does not establish a complete business workflow; its behavior needs review in the particular application and environment being used.
02

## A managed service adds business responsibility.
A Mission Canvas service engagement defines a business workflow, builds the required solution, and agrees the responsibilities for its ongoing care.
Using the desktop application and commissioning that service are separate choices, with different setup requirements, scope, and expectations for ongoing support.
03

## Review the application in your own environment.
Check the current installation guidance and requirements before trying the application, then evaluate the particular tasks you need it to support.
For business use, discuss access, connected accounts, operating limits, and care arrangements before depending on the application for an important workflow.

Source: https://pretendhome.github.io/press

For writers and partners

# Custom software with an ongoing service relationship.
Mission Canvas is developing a Customized Software as a Service offering for businesses that need software shaped around their own workflows.
01

## The proposed offering.
The approach combines a scoped custom software build with recurring care, using reusable infrastructure for capabilities that different workflows may share.
An engagement would define the business outcome, delivery scope, acceptance criteria, integrations, and ongoing responsibilities in a proposal for that business.
02

## How to describe Mission Canvas.
Mission Canvas focuses on the relationship between a business workflow, the software that supports it, and the people responsible for its care.
Customized Software as a Service, or CSaaS, is the name used here for bringing custom development and ongoing care into one engagement.
03

## Product and service boundaries.
Palette is an associated desktop foundation and development application; its application capabilities and installation guidance are distinct from the proposed managed service.
The industry workflows on this site illustrate possible scopes for discussion and do not represent customer testimonials or completed industry products.
A little more detail

## Questions worth asking.
Are commercial terms published?
The proposed service is scoped by quote, with final pricing, delivery terms, support arrangements, and outside costs agreed for each engagement. Are the industry examples customer case studies?
The examples illustrate workflows that could be scoped and built; they do not establish customer deployments, measured outcomes, or finished products. How should product claims be checked?
Ask for evidence tied to the particular application, workflow, and environment being discussed before describing a capability as available or proven.
Your next step

## Request a focused company conversation.
Describe the topic you are covering and the product or service facts you need to confirm for your audience.
Let’s talk about your work

A proposal shaped around your scope

# Agree the work. Understand the ongoing cost.
Our proposed service combines a scoped setup and build with recurring care, with final terms and figures set by quote.
01

## A defined setup and build.
The initial proposal describes the workflow, interfaces, integrations, acceptance criteria, and delivery responsibilities included in the agreed build scope.
The quote should make assumptions and exclusions visible, so you can judge the cost against the work you actually need.

### Workflow and requirements
The proposal identifies the people involved, the information required, and the decisions that the software needs to support.

### Build and review
The scope explains what will be delivered, how your team will review it, and which acceptance conditions need to be met.

### A practical handover
The agreement sets out the documentation, access, and operating responsibilities needed for your team to use the software confidently.
02

## Recurring care with a clear boundary.
An ongoing agreement can cover maintenance, support, and an agreed allowance or process for improvements as your business needs change.
The proposal defines the care period, included work, response arrangements, review process, and how additional requests will be priced and approved.
03

## Keep outside costs visible.
Hosting, third-party subscriptions, model usage, and other external services are separate costs unless your written quote explicitly includes them.
This proposed offer has no published standard rate or established service-level commitment; the final commercial model depends on your agreed scope.
A little more detail

## Questions worth asking.
Is there a standard monthly price?
Final figures and the billing model are subject to quote, based on the workflow, integrations, operating needs, and agreed care scope. How are larger changes handled?
We assess the request against the existing agreement and provide a separate scope and quote when the work falls outside it. What should an agreement explain?
It should explain payment, ownership, access, support, outside costs, cancellation, and the practical steps for handing the software over.
Your next step

## Get a proposal for your workflow.
Tell us what your team needs to accomplish, which systems are involved, and how the work is handled today.
Let’s talk about your work

Source: https://pretendhome.github.io/privacy

Website privacy · Updated 23 October 2026

# Your information, in plain words.
This website helps you understand the service and start a conversation. Project data arrangements are agreed separately for each implementation.

## What this website does.
The enquiry form prepares a draft in your own email application. It does not submit the form to a server or store your entries on this website.
We receive the information only if you choose to send the message. Your email provider handles the message according to its own arrangements.
This version of the site runs no analytics scripts and sets no application tracking cookies. GitHub Pages hosts these pages and records visitor IP addresses for security purposes. See GitHub’s hosting information ↗.

## Starting a conversation.
We use the information you send to respond to your enquiry and discuss the workflow. Please avoid sending confidential business records or sensitive personal information in an initial message.
No appointment calendar is embedded in this site. We arrange a suitable next step directly after an enquiry.

## Your project’s information.
A project scope should identify the data involved, where it is processed, who may access it and which external services are connected.
Hosting, support access, retention, export and transition arrangements are agreed for the implementation. Local deployment does not remove the need to understand external connections.
We do not treat permission to maintain software as permission to reuse a customer’s private records for other customers or model training.

## Questions and requests.
For a question about information you have sent us, contact jason.covington@missioncanvas.ai. Describe the request without including unnecessary sensitive details.

Source: https://pretendhome.github.io/security

Make the boundaries clear

# Decide who can see information and act on it.
Security requirements belong in the project scope, alongside the workflow, integrations, responsibilities, and evidence needed before everyday use begins.
01

## Start with the information your workflow needs.
We identify the information involved, where it will be processed, who needs access, and which connected services will receive it.
Access rules, retention, exports, and account responsibilities should be documented in the agreement and checked against your actual operating requirements.
02

## Keep consequential actions under clear authority.
The project should define which actions people can request, which require review, and what information is recorded when they happen.
Our reusable foundation includes source-linked work, version history, scoped access, and recorded actions; each implementation still needs its own validation.

### Access
Agree which people and connected accounts can reach the information needed for the workflow, and how that access is removed.

### Action
Define the authority needed for sending messages, changing records, or affecting another system, including what happens when an outcome is uncertain.

### Evidence
Choose the activity records, source references, and change history your team needs to review work and investigate a problem.
03

## Match claims to the implementation.
Hosting, local processing, provider access, backup arrangements, and recovery procedures depend on the solution and must be specified for the engagement.
We do not make a blanket compliance or certification claim; regulated requirements need specialist review and explicit acceptance before use.
Your next step

## Bring your requirements into the first conversation.
Share the access, hosting, review, and recordkeeping conditions your business needs so they can shape the scope from the start.
Let’s talk about your work

Source: https://pretendhome.github.io/what-is-mission-canvas

Customized Software as a Service

# Your workflow, made into software and cared for over time.
Mission Canvas is developing a service that combines software built for a particular business with ongoing maintenance, support, and improvement.
01

## A service shaped around a business outcome.
The project starts with something your team needs to accomplish, then defines the information, decisions, and handoffs required to get there.
The resulting software can bring those steps together in a focused workspace, with connections to existing systems where the scope allows.
02

## Custom work on a reusable foundation.
Shared infrastructure provides a starting point for common capabilities, while the interfaces, business rules, and workflow are shaped for your situation.
The foundation includes mechanisms for source-linked work, versions, scoped access, and recorded actions, with suitability verified for each proposed implementation.
03

## An agreement for what happens next.
The service model includes a scoped build and an ongoing care agreement, with responsibilities and commercial terms defined in your proposal.
You should be able to understand the software's purpose, judge the delivered result, and know how to request help or changes.
Your next step

## Find a useful first scope.
Describe the recurring work your team wants to improve and the outcome that would make a meaningful difference to them.
Let’s talk about your work

Source: https://pretendhome.github.io/why-mission-canvas

Fit, responsibility, and continuity

# Give important workflows a software owner.
Our proposed CSaaS approach connects a focused custom build with the care needed as systems, people, and business requirements change.
01

## Fit the software to the work.
We begin with the way your team handles a task, including the exceptions and judgments that a generic process can miss.
The first scope should solve a recognizable problem and give the people doing the work a clear way to judge progress.
02

## Keep the work understandable.
Sources, changes, access, and external actions need clear treatment so your team can understand the software's behavior and question its results.
We bring reusable mechanisms for those concerns and agree the review steps and evidence your particular workflow needs before use.
03

## Account for the work after delivery.
An ongoing agreement provides a place for maintenance, support, and agreed improvements, with boundaries that make the commitment understandable to both sides.
The proposal should explain ownership, outside services, change requests, and handover so the relationship remains practical as your business evolves.
Your next step

## See whether the approach fits.
Bring a recurring task and we can discuss the software, responsibilities, and ongoing care that a focused solution would require.
Let’s talk about your work
